questions.question: What is mocking in unit testing and why do we need it?
questions.title: What is Mocking in Unit Testing | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Mocking replaces a real dependency with a controlled fake that you configure to return specific values. It isolates the class under test from its dependencies—database, external APIs, file system—so you test only the unit's logic, not its dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that mocking is fundamentally about isolation and testing boundaries, not about making tests easier to pass.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking mocking is a shortcut to avoid writing real implementations, missing that it's about decoupling test scope from external systems.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain a concrete scenario where a failing database connection would break hundreds of unit tests if dependencies weren't mocked, showing you understand the practical need.

sections.title: Mocking: Controlled Isolation for Unit Tests
sections.content:
Mocking is the practice of replacing real dependencies with **test doubles** that behave exactly how you configure them. Imagine testing a **payment service** that talks to a bank API—you don't want your unit tests to actually charge credit cards or depend on the bank's server being online.

A **mock object** pretends to be that bank API, returning success or failure responses on command. This isolation means your test only exercises the payment service's logic: does it handle success correctly? Does it retry on failure? Does it log errors? The WHY is critical: without mocking, a database downtime or network issue would fail hundreds of unrelated tests, making it impossible to tell if your code is broken or the infrastructure is. Mocking draws a **boundary** around the unit under test, keeping external system failures out of your test results. The mock is a **puppet** you control—you tell it what to return, then verify your code reacts correctly.

sections.content:

blue|Why We Need It|~Isolation of the unit|no database or network|fast, deterministic tests|failures point to your code
emerald|What to Mock|~Things with side effects|repositories, REST clients|email senders, queues|never plain value objects

sections.title: Mocking a Repository in a Service Test
When to Mock Dependencies
sections.content: Use mocking when the dependency has **side effects** you can't control in a test: database queries, HTTP calls to external APIs, file system writes, message queue publishes, or time-based operations. Mock when the real dependency is **slow**—a unit test suite that hits a real database might take 10 minutes instead of 10 seconds. Mock when the dependency is **unreliable** in test environments: third-party APIs that throttle requests, services that aren't available in CI pipelines, or external systems that require complex authentication. In a Spring Boot service, you'd mock **repositories** (to avoid database setup), **REST clients** (to avoid network calls), and **email senders** (to avoid sending real emails during tests).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking value objects**: Freshers mock DTOs, POJOs, or simple data classes that have no behavior—like mocking a `Product` object with just getters. These should be real instances created with `new Product(...)` because they have no side effects.
- **Mocking the class under test**: Some beginners mock the service they're testing, then wonder why their test passes even when the real method is broken. You mock the dependencies, never the subject.
- **Thinking mocks make tests easier**: Mocking isn't a shortcut—it's a surgical tool to isolate behavior. Over-mocking can make tests harder to understand and maintain because you're testing mock configurations instead of real logic.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Isolation**: Mocking removes external dependencies so tests run fast and don't fail due to infrastructure issues
- **Test double**: The generic term for any fake object; a mock is one specific type that also verifies method calls
- **Side effects**: Mock things that talk to external systems—databases, APIs, file systems, queues
- **Configuration**: Use when-thenReturn to set up what the mock returns when called
- **Verification**: Use verify to assert that the dependency was called with expected arguments
- **Speed**: A unit test suite with mocked dependencies runs in seconds; with real dependencies it can take minutes
- **Scope boundary**: Mocking enforces the unit in unit test—you test one class's logic, not the entire integration stack

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mocking is replacing a real dependency with a fake one that you control. You'd say: It's about isolation. When I test a service, I don't want the test to fail because the database is down or an external API is slow. I mock those dependencies so the test only exercises the service's logic. For example, if I'm testing an order service that fetches data from a repository, I'd mock the repository to return a specific order. Then I test that the service calculates the total price correctly. The mock gives me control—I can make it return success, failure, empty data, whatever scenario I need. Without mocking, every test would need a running database, test data setup, and network access. That's slow and brittle. The key thing is mocking draws a boundary. I'm testing the order service, not the repository or the database driver. If the repository has its own bugs, that's a different test. This keeps tests fast and focused. One pitfall freshers hit is mocking everything, even simple value objects like a product DTO. You only mock things with side effects—external systems, I-O operations, things outside your control. If it's a plain data class, just create a real instance.

questions.question: What is Mockito and how do you add it to a Spring Boot project?
questions.title: Mockito Setup Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Mockito is the standard Java mocking library. In Spring Boot, spring-boot-starter-test includes Mockito automatically. Add at-ExtendsWith MockitoExtension.class to your test class to enable at-Mock and at-InjectMocks annotations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical setup knowledge—can you use Mockito in a real Spring Boot project without fumbling with dependencies or configuration?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually adding Mockito as a separate Maven dependency when spring-boot-starter-test already includes it, creating version conflicts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that spring-boot-starter-test uses test scope, so Mockito never pollutes production artifacts, and name the specific JUnit 5 extension class.

sections.title: Mockito: The Standard Java Mocking Framework
sections.content:
**Mockito** is the industry-standard mocking library for Java, used in over 90% of Java projects according to GitHub trends. It provides a fluent API for creating mock objects, stubbing method calls, and verifying interactions.

The beauty of Mockito is its **readability**—tests read like plain English: `when(userRepository.findById(1)).thenReturn(user)`. In a Spring Boot project, you don't need to add Mockito manually. The **spring-boot-starter-test** dependency bundles Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and other testing tools. To activate Mockito in a JUnit 5 test, you annotate the class with `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)`. This extension initializes mocks annotated with `@Mock` and injects them into the class under test annotated with `@InjectMocks`. Think of Mockito as a **puppet master** for your dependencies—it creates lightweight fake objects that respond exactly how you program them, without any real behavior.

sections.content:
amber|Mockito|~Standard Java mock library|fluent when then return|the Mock annotation|the InjectMocks annotation
blue|Already Bundled|~spring-boot-starter-test|includes Mockito and JUnit 5|test scope only|no manual dependency
emerald|Activate It|~JUnit 5 extension|the ExtendWith MockitoExtension|inits the Mock fields|injects into the subject

sections.title: Setting Up Mockito in a Spring Boot Test
When You Already Have Mockito
sections.content:
If your Spring Boot project has **spring-boot-starter-test** in the dependencies block (which every new Spring Boot project includes by default), Mockito is already on the classpath. You'll use Mockito in **unit tests** for services, controllers, and components that have dependencies you want to isolate. For example, testing a `UserService` that depends on `UserRepository` and `EmailService`—you'd mock both dependencies to test the service logic without hitting a database or sending real emails.

Use `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` on JUnit 5 test classes, or `@RunWith(MockitoJUnitRunner.class)` if you're stuck on JUnit 4. For Spring integration tests with `@SpringBootTest`, you'd use `@MockBean` instead, which registers mocks in the Spring application context—but that's integration testing, not pure unit testing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Adding Mockito manually**: Freshers see Mockito in code examples and add it as a separate Maven dependency, not realizing spring-boot-starter-test already includes it. This creates version conflicts because you end up with two different Mockito versions on the classpath.
- **Forgetting the extension**: Writing `@Mock` and `@InjectMocks` but not adding `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` to the test class—Mockito never initializes, so all mocks are null and tests crash with NullPointerException.
- **Using test scope wrong**: Some beginners add Mockito with compile scope instead of test, which bundles Mockito into production artifacts, bloating the JAR unnecessarily.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **spring-boot-starter-test**: Includes Mockito, JUnit 5, AssertJ, and Hamcrest—no need to add Mockito separately
- **MockitoExtension**: JUnit 5 extension class that initializes mocks before each test method runs
- **at-Mock**: Creates a mock instance of the annotated type; all methods return default values until stubbed
- **at-InjectMocks**: Creates a real instance and injects all at-Mock fields into it via constructor or field injection
- **Test scope**: Mockito dependency is marked with scope test, so it never gets packaged in production builds
- **Fluent API**: Mockito uses method chaining—when, thenReturn, verify—that reads like natural language
- **Version management**: Spring Boot's dependency management plugin ensures compatible Mockito version; never override it manually

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Mockito is the standard mocking library for Java. It's what most companies use for unit testing. In Spring Boot, you don't need to add it yourself—it's already included in spring-boot-starter-test, which every Spring Boot project has by default. To use Mockito in a JUnit 5 test, you add at-ExtendsWith MockitoExtension dot class at the top of your test class. That activates Mockito's annotation processing. Then you annotate your dependencies with at-Mock, which tells Mockito to create fake instances. You annotate the class you're testing with at-InjectMocks, and Mockito injects the mocks into it. So if you're testing a user service that needs a user repository, you'd write at-Mock UserRepository and at-InjectMocks UserService. Mockito creates a fake repository and plugs it into the real service. One thing freshers get wrong is manually adding Mockito as a Maven dependency. Spring Boot already manages the version through spring-boot-starter-test, so adding it again creates conflicts. Another mistake is forgetting the extension annotation—without at-ExtendsWith, the mocks are null because Mockito never initializes them. The key benefit is that Mockito stays in test scope, so it never gets packaged into your production JAR.

questions.question: When should you NOT mock a dependency?
questions.title: When Not to Mock | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Don't mock value objects, simple utilities, or classes you own that have no side effects. Don't mock the class under test itself. Don't mock thin wrappers that are trivially tested with real implementation. Over-mocking produces tests that test the test setup, not the code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Testing judgment—knowing the limits of mocking is as important as knowing how to use it; good engineers know when NOT to apply a tool.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking everything including simple value classes, DTOs, and pure functions, which wastes setup time and tests nothing real.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'mock only what you don't own' guideline from Growing Object-Oriented Software and explain when integration tests are better than heavily mocked unit tests.

sections.title: When Mocking Does More Harm Than Good
sections.content:
Not every dependency deserves a mock. Mocking is a **surgical tool** for isolating side effects, but freshers often treat it like a hammer and mock everything in sight. The fundamental guideline: **mock only what you don't own**—dependencies whose implementation you can't see or control, like external APIs, databases, or third-party libraries. When you mock a class you wrote, you're testing your assumptions about how it should behave, not how it actually behaves. That's a **test illusion**—the test passes but production might fail because your mock's behavior doesn't match reality. Value objects, DTOs, simple calculators, and pure functions should be **real instances** in tests. They're cheap to create, have no side effects, and their behavior is what you want to verify.

Think of it this way: if the dependency is **simpler than the mock setup**, use the real thing. Over-mocking is a red flag that you're writing tests that exercise mock configurations instead of real code paths.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Don't Mock|~No side effects, use real|DTOs and records|pure utilities|the class under test
blue|Ownership Rule|~Mock what you don't own|third-party libraries|framework classes|use real for your code
emerald|Smell Signals|~Too many mocks|setup longer than asserts|prefer an integration test|split the class

sections.title: Code Example
Step 1: Ask If It Has Side Effects
sections.content: The first decision: does this dependency perform I-O, talk to external systems, or modify shared state? If yes, consider mocking. Examples: **database repositories** (network I-O, persistent state), **HTTP clients** (external service calls), **message queue publishers** (asynchronous side effects), **file writers** (disk I-O). These are slow, unreliable in test environments, or require complex setup. If no side effects, use the real class. Examples: **DTOs and value objects** (just data containers), **utility classes** (pure functions like StringUtils), **domain models** (business logic with no I-O), **builders and factories** (object creation with no state). Testing with real instances here is faster and more accurate than mocking.

sections.title: Step 2: Apply the Ownership Test
sections.content: If you own the code—meaning it's in your codebase and you can read and modify it—default to using the real implementation unless it has side effects. This guideline comes from **Growing Object-Oriented Software Guided by Tests**: mock types you don't own, use real implementations for types you do own. Why? When you mock your own code, you're testing against an assumption. If the real class changes behavior, your mock won't, and tests will pass while production breaks. For third-party libraries and frameworks, you don't control the implementation, so mocking is safer. Example: mock `RestTemplate` (Spring's HTTP client) because you don't own it, but don't mock your own `PriceCalculator` class—write a test that exercises the real calculator.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking DTOs and records**: Freshers mock data transfer objects like `OrderDTO` or Java records, which are pure data with no behavior. Creating a real instance with `new OrderDTO(...)` is simpler and tests the actual structure.
- **Mocking the subject**: Some beginners mock the very class they're testing, then stub its methods. This tests nothing—the mock's behavior is what you programmed, not what the code does.
- **Mocking simple utilities**: Mocking a `StringUtils.trim()` or `Math.max()` method when the real method is instant and has no side effects. This adds complexity for zero benefit and obscures what the test is actually verifying.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Side effects rule**: Mock dependencies that perform I-O, network calls, or modify shared state; use real instances otherwise
- **Ownership guideline**: Mock types you don't own (third-party libraries, frameworks); use real implementations for code you control
- **Value objects**: Never mock DTOs, POJOs, records, or data classes—they're trivial to instantiate and have no behavior
- **Integration tests**: When mocking becomes complex with many dependencies, consider an integration test with a real lightweight stack
- **Test accuracy**: Mocking your own code tests your assumptions, not reality; if the real class changes, the mock won't reflect it
- **Setup cost**: If writing the mock setup is harder than using the real dependency, you're over-engineering the test
- **Class under test**: Never mock the class you're testing—mock its dependencies, test the real subject

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: You should not mock things that have no side effects or are simpler than the mock setup. The main rule is: mock what you don't own. If it's a third-party library or a framework class, mocking makes sense because you don't control the implementation. But if it's your own code, use the real class unless it hits a database or external system. For example, don't mock a DTO or a record. Those are just data containers. Creating a real instance with new is easier and tests the actual structure. Don't mock simple utilities like string helpers or math functions. They're fast, predictable, and have no side effects. And never mock the class you're testing. I see freshers do this—they mock the service they're testing, then wonder why the test passes even when the real method is broken. You mock the dependencies, not the subject. Another case is when you have too many mocks. If you're mocking five or six dependencies, that's a sign your test is too complex. Maybe the class has too many responsibilities, or maybe you need an integration test instead. The classic guideline from Growing Object-Oriented Software is: only mock types you don't own. If you own it and can see the source, use the real thing. That way, if the real class changes behavior, your test catches it.

questions.question: What is the difference between mocking and stubbing?
questions.title: Mocking vs Stubbing Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Stubbing configures a fake to return a specific value using when-thenReturn. Mocking in the verification sense asserts that a method was called using verify. Mockito objects are both—they can stub return values AND verify interactions. The terms are often used interchangeably in casual speech.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise vocabulary around test doubles and whether you know the technical distinction even though Mockito blurs the line.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using mock and stub interchangeably without knowing that stub is about return values and mock is about call verification.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Reference Gerard Meszaros's test double taxonomy and explain that Mockito's unified approach is pragmatic but technically a mock is a stub with verification.

sections.title: Stubbing vs Mocking: Two Sides of Test Doubles
sections.content:
In testing terminology, **stubbing** and **mocking** are related but distinct concepts, though Mockito blurs the line for practical reasons. **Stubbing** is about controlling what a fake object returns—you program it to give specific answers when called. A **stub** is a test double that responds with canned data: `when(repo.findById(1)).thenReturn(user)`.

You're setting up the dependency's output. **Mocking** in the strict sense is about verifying interactions—asserting that a method was called with expected arguments: `verify(repo).save(user)`. A **mock** is a test double that records calls and lets you assert on them. Here's the twist: Mockito objects do both. When you create a Mockito mock, you can stub its methods AND verify calls. So in practice, people say mock when they mean stub, and that's fine in conversation. But knowing the technical distinction shows depth: stubs answer questions, mocks verify behavior.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Stubbing|~Control return values|when then return|focuses on queries|state-based testing
blue|Mocking (strict)|~Verify interactions|the verify call|focuses on commands|interaction-based testing
emerald|Mockito Reality|~One object does both|stub then verify|terms used loosely|know the distinction

sections.title: Code Example
Stub vs Mock
sections.content:
| Aspect | Stub | Mock |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Provide canned answers to calls | Verify method calls happened |
| Setup | when-thenReturn configures return values | No setup needed for verification |
| Assertion | Test asserts on results from subject | Test asserts on interactions with stub |
| Failure mode | Test fails if subject logic wrong | Test fails if expected call missing |
| Mockito syntax | when repo dot find then return user | verify repo dot save was called |

sections.title: When to Stub vs When to Verify
sections.content:
Use **stubbing** when you need to control what a dependency returns so you can test the subject's logic. Example: stubbing a repository to return a specific user so you can test that your service calculates the user's age correctly. The focus is on the **return value** and how the subject reacts to it.

Use **verification** when the important behavior is that the subject called the dependency, not what it returned. Example: verifying that an email service's `send()` method was called when a password reset happens. The side effect matters, not a return value. In Mockito, you'll often do both in the same test: stub the repository to return data, then verify the service called the repository. This is **state-based testing** (assert on results) combined with **interaction-based testing** (assert on calls).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using mock to mean stub**: Freshers say 'I mocked the return value' when they mean 'I stubbed it.' Technically, mocking is verification, not return configuration. This matters in code reviews where seniors expect precise vocabulary.
- **Over-verifying**: Beginners verify every single method call, including internal details that aren't part of the contract. This makes tests brittle—refactoring the implementation breaks tests even when behavior is unchanged.
- **Not verifying side effects**: When testing a method that should send an email or publish an event, freshers only stub but never verify the call happened. The test passes even if the side effect is removed from production code.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Stub**: Test double configured to return specific values; focuses on query methods that return data
- **Mock (strict)**: Test double that verifies interactions; focuses on command methods with side effects
- **Mockito unifies**: A Mockito mock object can be stubbed with when-thenReturn and verified with verify
- **State-based testing**: Assert on the result the subject returns after calling stubbed dependencies
- **Interaction-based testing**: Assert that the subject called the dependency's methods in the right way
- **Verification syntax**: verify takes the mock and asserts a method was called, optionally with specific arguments
- **Gerard Meszaros taxonomy**: Defines five test double types—dummy, stub, spy, mock, fake—Mockito combines several

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Stubbing and mocking are related but different. Stubbing is when you configure a fake object to return a specific value. You use when-thenReturn to set up what it gives back. For example, when repository dot find by I-D returns a user object. That's stubbing—you're controlling the answer. Mocking in the strict sense is about verifying that a method was called. You use verify to assert the interaction happened. For example, verify repository dot save was called with this user. That's mocking—you're checking behavior, not return values. The confusing part is that Mockito blurs this distinction. A Mockito mock can do both—you stub its return values and verify its calls. So people casually say mock when they mean stub, and that's fine in conversation. But knowing the difference matters in interviews. Stubbing is about queries—methods that return data. Mocking is about commands—methods with side effects. If you're testing that a service calculates a total correctly, you stub the repository. If you're testing that the service sends an email, you verify the email service was called. In practice, you often do both in one test. Stub the dependencies to return test data, then verify the subject called the right methods. The key thing is: stub focuses on what came back, verify focuses on what was called.

questions.question: What is the difference between a test double and a mock?
questions.title: Test Double vs Mock
questions.direct_answer: Test double is the umbrella term for any fake object used in testing; a mock is a specific type of test double that also verifies interactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand testing vocabulary precisely and know that Mockito blurs some of these boundaries for pragmatic reasons.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using mock and test double interchangeably when they have distinct meanings in Martin Fowler's and Gerard Meszaros's taxonomies.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name all five categories of test doubles—dummy, stub, fake, spy, mock—and explain where Mockito fits (spy with mock-like verification).

sections.title: Test Doubles: The Full Taxonomy
sections.content:
**Test double** is the umbrella term coined by **Gerard Meszaros** for any object that stands in for a real dependency in a test.

Think of it like stunt doubles in movies—they look like the actor but are controlled fakes. There are five types: **dummy** (passed but never used), **stub** (returns canned answers), **spy** (records calls while delegating to real object), **mock** (verifies interactions), and **fake** (working lightweight implementation). A **mock** is one specific kind of test double that asserts method calls happened. In strict terminology, not all test doubles are mocks—a stub only provides return values without verification. Mockito's naming is pragmatic but technically imprecise: what Mockito calls a mock is closer to a **spy with verification**. It can stub return values like a stub, verify calls like a mock, and even delegate to real methods like a spy. Understanding this taxonomy matters because it shows you know the theory behind the tools, not just the syntax.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Test Double|~Umbrella term|any stand-in fake|coined by Meszaros|five sub-types
blue|The Five Types|~Each has a job|dummy, stub, fake|spy and mock|mock verifies calls
emerald|Where Mockito Fits|~A hybrid object|stubs like a stub|verifies like a mock|spies a real object

sections.title: Code Example
Test Double Types
sections.content:
| Type | Purpose | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dummy | Fills parameter list, never used | Passing null or empty object to satisfy signature |
| Stub | Returns pre-programmed answers | Repository returning fixed test data |
| Spy | Records calls, optionally delegates to real | Mockito spy wrapping real object |
| Mock | Verifies methods were called | Asserting email service send was invoked |
| Fake | Working implementation, simplified | In-memory database instead of real SQL |

sections.title: When to Use Each Test Double
sections.content:
Use a **dummy** when a method signature requires an argument but the test doesn't care about it—often you just pass `null` or an empty object.

Use a **stub** when you need to control return values to test logic paths: stubbing a repository to return a specific user so you can test access control.

Use a **spy** when you want mostly real behavior but need to verify one specific call or stub one method: testing a service with real helper methods but a stubbed external API call.

Use a **mock** when the key assertion is that a side effect occurred: verifying an audit log was written or a message was published.

Use a **fake** when the real dependency is too heavy but you want realistic behavior: an in-memory H2 database instead of PostgreSQL, or a local queue instead of Kafka. In practice, Mockito mocks cover 80% of cases because they can stub and verify, reducing the need to distinguish stub from mock.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling everything a mock**: Freshers use mock as a synonym for test double, missing that it's a specific type with verification semantics. This leads to confusion when someone says 'don't mock value objects' and they think it means 'don't use any test doubles.' **Not knowing spy exists**: Beginners overuse full mocks when a spy would be better—testing a class where most methods are real but one needs stubbing. Mockito's `spy()` lets you wrap a real instance and selectively stub methods.
- **Ignoring fakes**: Some tests end up with dozens of mock setups when a simple fake would be clearer. Example: mocking every method of a map when you could just use a real HashMap, or mocking a repository with complex state when an in-memory implementation would be more readable.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Test double**: Umbrella term for any fake object in testing—coined by Gerard Meszaros in xUnit Test Patterns
- **Five types**: Dummy (unused), stub (returns values), spy (records calls), mock (verifies calls), fake (working lightweight)
- **Mock specificity**: In strict terminology, a mock verifies interactions—not all test doubles do this
- **Mockito blurs lines**: A Mockito mock can stub like a stub and verify like a mock, combining multiple roles
- **Spy use case**: When you need real behavior but want to verify one method was called or stub one dependency
- **Fake advantage**: More realistic than stubs for complex stateful dependencies like databases or queues
- **Martin Fowler distinction**: Separates mocks (behavior verification) from stubs (state verification) in his 2007 article

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Test double is the general term for any fake object you use in a test. It's the category. A mock is one specific type of test double. The taxonomy comes from Gerard Meszaros's book on test patterns. There are five kinds. A dummy is an object you pass to satisfy a method signature but never actually use—like passing null for a parameter the test doesn't care about. A stub returns pre-programmed values. When you write when repository dot find by I-D then return user, that's a stub. A spy records what methods were called and can optionally delegate to the real object. Mockito's spy method wraps a real instance. A mock verifies interactions. When you write verify email service dot send, you're using a mock—it asserts the method was called. A fake is a working lightweight implementation, like an in-memory database instead of the real one. Now, Mockito blurs these lines. What Mockito calls a mock can actually stub and verify, so it's kind of a hybrid. That's pragmatic because most tests need both—stub the return values and verify the calls. The key distinction is that not every test double verifies interactions, so not everything is technically a mock. Freshers often say mock when they mean any test double, but knowing the taxonomy shows you understand the theory. In practice, you'd say I'm using a Mockito mock, and everyone knows you mean a test double that can do both stubbing and verification.

questions.question: What is the difference between state-based testing and interaction-based testing, and where does mocking fit?
questions.title: State vs Interaction Testing
questions.direct_answer: State-based testing asserts on the final state of an object; interaction-based testing, where mocking lives, asserts that the right collaborators were called in the right way.

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of understanding of why mocking exists as a concept and when it's the appropriate testing strategy versus state verification.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating every test as interaction-based and over-verifying internal calls, making tests brittle and coupled to implementation.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that interaction tests are fragile and should be reserved for side-effect boundaries like external APIs or messaging, not internal logic.

sections.title: State vs Interaction: Two Testing Philosophies
sections.content:
**State-based testing** and **interaction-based testing** represent two fundamentally different ways to verify correctness. **State-based** testing, the classical approach, asserts on the result or final state of the system after an operation. You call a method, then check that the return value is correct or that the object's state changed as expected.

Example: calling `orderService.calculateTotal()` and asserting the returned price is 120 dollars. You're verifying **what happened**, not **how it happened**. **Interaction-based testing** asserts on the calls made to collaborators during execution. You use mocks to verify that the subject called specific methods with specific arguments. Example: verifying that `emailService.send()` was called when a user registers. You're verifying **how the system collaborated**, not the end result. Mocking lives in the interaction-based world. The trade-off: state tests are resilient to refactoring (you can change internal implementation without breaking tests), but interaction tests are better for verifying side effects that don't return values.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|State-Based|~Assert the result|return value or state|refactor-friendly|JUnit assertions
blue|Interaction-Based|~Assert the calls|the verify call|where mocking lives|coupled to structure
emerald|How to Choose|~Default to state|interaction at boundaries|side effects only|don't over-verify

sections.title: Code Example
State-Based vs Interaction-Based Testing
sections.content:
| Aspect | State-Based | Interaction-Based |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it verifies | Final result or object state | Method calls to collaborators |
| Assertion style | assertEquals, assertTrue on results | verify mock method was called |
| Refactoring resilience | High—implementation can change | Low—coupled to call structure |
| Use case | Business logic, calculations, transforms | Side effects, I-O, external systems |
| Typical tool | JUnit assertions, AssertJ | Mockito verify, argument captors |

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **state-based testing** for business logic, calculations, and transformations where you care about the outcome, not the internal steps. Example: testing a pricing engine that calculates discounts—assert on the final price, not on whether it called a tax calculator internally. State tests are **refactoring-friendly** because you can change the implementation without breaking tests.

Use **interaction-based testing** for side effects that don't return useful values: sending emails, publishing events, writing audit logs, calling external APIs. Example: verifying that a password reset triggered an email—there's no return value to assert on, so you verify the email service was called. Interaction tests are **fragile** because they couple to implementation structure. If you refactor how the code calls its dependencies, interaction tests break even if behavior is unchanged. The guideline: default to state-based, use interaction-based only at **system boundaries** where side effects matter.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Over-verifying internal calls**: Freshers verify every method call on every dependency, including internal helpers that are implementation details. This makes tests brittle—refactoring a private method breaks tests even though public behavior is unchanged.
- **Not verifying side effects**: When testing a method that should send a notification or log an audit entry, beginners only assert the return value and forget to verify the side effect happened.
- **Mixing styles inconsistently**: Some tests assert on state and verify interactions for the same operation, creating redundant assertions that obscure what's actually being tested. Pick one style per test case—either assert the outcome or verify the collaboration, not both unless necessary.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **State-based**: Asserts on return values or object state after an operation—answers 'what is the result'
- **Interaction-based**: Asserts on method calls to collaborators—answers 'how did it interact'
- **Refactoring resilience**: State tests survive implementation changes; interaction tests break when call structure changes
- **Side-effect verification**: Interaction tests are best for verifying I-O or external calls that don't return values
- **Fragility trade-off**: Interaction tests couple to implementation details, making them brittle under refactoring
- **System boundaries**: Use interaction tests at edges—external APIs, databases, messaging—not internal logic
- **Martin Fowler distinction**: His 2007 article on mocks vs stubs popularized the state vs interaction terminology

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: State-based testing is when you assert on the result or final state of an object. You call a method and check what it returned or how the object changed. For example, testing a calculator—you call calculate total and assert the result is one-twenty. You don't care how it computed the value, just that it's correct. That's state-based. Interaction-based testing is when you verify that the right methods were called on collaborators. You use mocks and write verify statements. For example, testing that a user registration sends a welcome email. You verify the email service's send method was called. You're checking the collaboration, not the return value. Mocking lives in the interaction world. The key difference is what you're verifying. State tests answer 'what happened,' interaction tests answer 'how did it happen.' State tests are better for refactoring because you can change the internal implementation and the test still passes. Interaction tests are fragile—if you refactor the calls, the test breaks even if behavior is unchanged. The guideline is: default to state-based. Use interaction-based only for side effects at system boundaries—external APIs, databases, messaging. Don't verify internal calls. Freshers often over-verify every method call, which couples the test to implementation details. If you refactor a private helper, the test shouldn't break. That's why interaction tests should be reserved for things like verifying an audit log was written or a message was published—side effects that don't return useful values.

questions.question: How does over-mocking harm a test suite, and how do you recognise it?
questions.title: Over-Mocking Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: Over-mocking means mocking classes you own and control, making tests pass even when real integration would fail, and tightly coupling tests to implementation details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the limits and risks of mocking; distinguishing engineers who understand when a tool is harmful from those who apply it everywhere.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mocking value objects, DTOs, or simple domain classes that have no side effects, resulting in tests that exercise mock configuration rather than code.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the 'only mock types you don't own' heuristic from Growing Object-Oriented Software and describe a concrete sign: test setup longer than test body.

sections.title: Over-Mocking: Testing the Test Setup
sections.content:
**Over-mocking** is when you mock so many dependencies that your test no longer exercises real code paths—it tests your mock configuration instead.

The core problem: mocking your own classes creates a **parallel universe** where the mock behaves how you think the class should behave, not how it actually behaves. If the real class changes—adds validation, throws an exception, changes return types—the mock doesn't, so tests keep passing while production breaks. This is **false confidence**: green tests that don't correlate with working code. A concrete smell: **test setup longer than test body**. If you spend 20 lines stubbing mocks and 3 lines asserting results, you're testing the mocks. Another smell: **mocking value objects**—DTOs, records, domain models with no side effects. These are trivial to instantiate and have no behavior to isolate. The guideline from **Growing Object-Oriented Software Guided by Tests** is clear: mock only types you don't own—external systems, third-party libraries, framework code. For your own classes, use real instances or refactor to reduce coupling.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Over-Mocking|~Mocking too much|your own classes|value objects|the subject itself
blue|The Harm|~False confidence|green but broken|brittle tests|tests the setup
emerald|Recognise It|~Setup beats asserts|five-plus mocks|refactor breaks tests|mock only seams

sections.title: Code Example
Recognising Over-Mocking in Practice
sections.content: You've over-mocked if **more than half your dependencies are mocked** and most are classes you own. Example: a service with five dependencies—four are mocked including a domain calculator and a DTO validator. That's a red flag. You've over-mocked if **setup is longer than assertions**—the test spends 15 lines on when-thenReturn and 2 lines on assertEquals. You've over-mocked if **tests pass but integration fails**—your mocks return success, but the real repository throws a constraint violation. You've over-mocked if **refactoring breaks tests**—you rename a private helper method and 10 tests fail because they verify that helper was called. The fix: mock only the **seams**—places where your code talks to external systems. For internal collaborations, use real objects or consider that the class has too many responsibilities and needs splitting.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking domain objects**: Freshers mock entities, value objects, and aggregates that represent business concepts. These are the core of the system—testing them with mocks tests nothing.
- **Mocking everything by default**: Some beginners add at-Mock to every field in the test class without asking if it's necessary. This creates a test suite where every test is heavily mocked and none exercise real interactions.
- **Not using integration tests**: When mocking becomes complex—five or six mocks per test—it's often a sign that an integration test with a real lightweight stack (like an in-memory database) would be clearer and more valuable than a heavily mocked unit test.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **False confidence**: Over-mocked tests pass even when production code is broken because mocks behave as programmed, not as reality
- **Parallel universe**: Mocks represent your assumptions; if real classes evolve, mocks don't, creating divergence
- **Setup smell**: Test setup longer than assertions is a concrete sign of over-mocking
- **Value objects**: Never mock DTOs, records, or data classes—they're trivial to create and have no side effects
- **Types you own**: Mocking your own domain logic tests your assumptions, not your code—use real instances
- **Seam boundaries**: Mock at system edges—databases, external APIs, file systems—not internal collaborators
- **Growing Object-Oriented Software**: The book's heuristic is 'only mock types you don't own' to avoid over-mocking internal logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Over-mocking harms a test suite because it creates tests that pass even when the code is broken. It happens when you mock classes you own instead of using real instances. If the real class changes behavior—like it adds validation or throws a new exception—the mock doesn't reflect that, so tests keep passing. That's false confidence. You think the code works because tests are green, but production might fail. One way to recognize over-mocking is the setup smell. If your test has twenty lines of when-then-return statements and three lines of assertions, you're testing the mock setup, not the code. Another sign is mocking value objects. Freshers mock DTOs, records, or domain models that are just data containers. Creating a real instance is simpler and tests the actual structure. A third sign is when you have to mock five or six dependencies per test. That's a red flag that the class has too many responsibilities or that you're mocking things you shouldn't. The guideline from Growing Object-Oriented Software is: only mock types you don't own. If it's a third-party library or framework code, mocking makes sense. But if it's your own code—domain logic, calculators, validators—use the real implementation unless it hits a database or external system. Another concrete indicator is when refactoring breaks tests. If you rename a private helper method and ten tests fail because they verify that method was called, your tests are too coupled to implementation. Interaction tests should verify public contracts at system boundaries, not internal details. The fix is to mock only the seams—the edges where your code talks to external systems—and let internal collaborations use real objects.
